name: Freya Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 58, lead developer at a small tech company that tracks chilled seafood deliveries. I have a master's degree and know the code well, but this firm pays less than most lead posts and there are few similar employers here. I use AI every day for test drafts, then check the driver's thermometer sheet. My partner works part-time at a hardware shop, our daughter has grown up, and we rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the fish sellers a cold-box warning is useful only if the thermometer and delivery time agree. I lead software for a tech company's seafood delivery app and use AI every day to draft tests, then check them against the driver's temperature sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI does little, I expect to keep the lead job, but money is tight already. I have a master's degree and strong technical skills, yet this small firm's pay is low for a lead; my partner works part-time at a hardware shop, we rent, and only three weeks of expenses are saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing missed cold-box alerts against the temperature sheets. We'd cancel the 29 monthly film channels and put that fee into a separate rent account whenever both incomes arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our bills, even with modest AI change. A spoiled box and a late rent payment both start with a number somebody failed to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to the fish box?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A box of fish reached the market at noon, but the driver's sheet showed it had warmed above the safe limit at ten. I kept the delivery warning open while the seller checked the box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your daughter help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter is training as an electrician and pays her own rent. I like that she learns a trade, but her wages are not our emergency fund.

I'd keep **unsafe deliveries** visible until sellers check the box.
think: I have **three weeks saved** despite leading the code team.
I earn **below usual lead pay** with few local software employers.
do: Keep **fixing missed cold-box alerts** against signed driver temperature sheets and seller checks.
Cancel **29 monthly film channels** and save the fee whenever both incomes arrive.
feel: **Anxious** about rent before strong AI arrives.

fieldNote: **Three weeks saved** and low lead pay explain baseline anxiety despite strong technical standing.

steps.text: Keep fixing cold-box alerts against signed driver temperature sheets
Save cancelled fee whenever both incomes arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could write delivery code and book routes, but the system must not turn a warm box into a green tick. I am happy to test a faster alert if the seller can reject a bad clearance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own lead hours could shrink if one team handles more shipments with the new tools. Three weeks saved is no cushion against a quiet pay cut, even if I can learn the tool quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the market manager to approve a two-week comparison of AI warnings with old anonymous temperature sheets, including the noon box and a properly chilled delivery. If it catches both without false clearance, I'd use it for one route with the seller able to stop dispatch; we'd delay replacing the kitchen table until my paid hours are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage, but I can run the comparison this month. I do not want a seller to find out at lunch that our green tick hid a warm box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cases must the tool distinguish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warm case must fail, and the properly chilled case must pass. If the tool calls every box unsafe, the market loses a day of trade and learns nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why can the table wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old table is scratched but sound. We can keep eating at it while we see whether my team still has the same hours.

say: I'd test **AI cold warnings** against real thermometer sheets.
I'd keep **seller stop power** before live route release.
think: I could lose **lead paid hours** even while I learn AI quickly.
I cannot absorb **a wage cut** on three weeks saved.
do: Trial **AI cold warnings** two weeks only with manager approval and both temperature cases.
Use on **one delivery route** only if cases pass and seller can stop dispatch.

feel: **Anxious** about income, willing to test a bounded route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write market code before unloading robots arrive around 2031. A seller still needs a way to challenge a false safe-temperature notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the lead software post could be cut fast, and my partner's part-time shop pay would not cover rent and food alone. Three weeks saved will not carry a long search, however good I am at the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the fish market and two nearby firms about actual paid cold-chain records or software vacancies, hours and wages. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed job whose pay with my partner's actual shop shifts covers rent, food and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek available paid local work and ask the landlord about timing before rent is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A cold box still has to be checked, but that does not create a salary for me at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a hiring manager the anonymised noon-box correction and the driver's temperature trail. It shows why the box needed a seller's inspection, not just a new line of code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your partner loses shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would check the new job's shift times against paid hardware-shop hours. If shop work is lost, my signed wage alone has to cover the rent and food.

say: I'd keep **seller appeals** if 2028 thinking AI replaces market code.
I'd check **actual paid vacancies** before naming another job.
think: I expect **my lead post** could go quickly.
I cannot cover **rent and food** on part-time shop pay alone.
do: Ask **market and two firms** about paid cold-chain and software openings.

If none qualifies, seek **available paid local work** and contact landlord before arrears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected loss of the main wage and three-week reserve.
S2.quote: A cold box still has to be checked, but that does not create a salary for me at the market.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches her software work before unloading robots arrive around 2031, threatening the main wage.
Physical cold checks do not guarantee **a paid vacancy** or income covering rent.

steps.text: Ask market and two local firms about paid cold-chain records and software jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 is enough to see whether the adult college will pay someone to teach cold-chain software checks. Thinking AI reaches my code then, with unloading robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could teach one evening class alongside my developer post. A classroom is not a wage unless the college hires me. I will not use the three-week rent reserve to set up a course or assume a full teaching job appears later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the adult college for posted paid instructor hours and ask my software employer whether outside teaching is allowed without losing my normal paid shifts. If the college offers a signed evening class, my employer permits it and my partner agrees to the evening schedule, I'd teach the thermometer-to-alert exercise for one term; after 2031 I'd keep it only while paid hours continue and seek a signed local job covering rent, food and travel if coding ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the main wage, but a real class could add modest income. I would rather teach someone to read a temperature sheet than sell a promise about coding forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the class teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Students would see the noon warm box and a chilled one, then decide whether the seller should accept the delivery. The lesson is that the record and the person at the market both matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your partner judge the rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would compare the college rota with shop hours and time together. If evening teaching costs paid shop shifts, we would need the net extra income to be positive before I accept.

I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches code before 2034 unloading robots.
think: I cannot treat **possible teaching** as current rent money.
I need **college pay** and employer permission without losing our main wages.

feel: **Anxious** about main income, willing to teach a paid practical class.
S3.quote: A classroom is not a wage unless the college hires me.
fieldNote: **Five years** support a possible paid evening class without assuming a full new teaching career.
Employer permission, **college pay**, partner agreement and positive net income gate the side work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 could bring me to 68, but thinking AI still reaches market software before unloading robots around 2039. A thermometer sheet should remain readable to anyone who pays for a fish delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have three weeks saved today and my partner's shop hours are part-time. I have no checked pension amount, so I cannot call a later teaching class or retirement cheque guaranteed income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cold-box cases and save the cancelled 29 film fee whenever both incomes arrive, then request both retirement statements and compare verified income with a full year of shop wages and rent. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if those figures cover rent, food and travel; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid work without counting our daughter's wages or an unoffered college class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today’s rent even with a decade. I would like the college idea to work. I will not put college teaching into the household budget before the first paid class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a later developer see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old noon-box case should remain in the test file with names removed. A younger developer should know why the green status was wrong even if the software writes the next test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter is learning her own trade. I want her to visit, not to fill a hole in a retirement spreadsheet.

I'd keep **real temperature evidence** beside future market software.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the main software wage could go before a paid market or college role appears. Written cut notice, real paid openings and a landlord conversation before arrears would help us keep rent current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether teaching a class would make me a professor. One paid evening term would help with bills, but it would not replace the software wage or make the rent disappear.

headlineQuote: One paid evening term would help with bills, but it would not replace the software wage or make the rent disappear.
portrait: Freya, **58**, leads chilled-seafood software after a master's degree and checks AI test drafts against driver temperature sheets.
Her **low lead pay**, partner's part-time shop work, three-week reserve and few nearby firms make rent precarious today.
She uses AI **daily**, but a one-route trial requires manager approval, contrasting temperature cases and seller stop power.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; a paid college class is conditional side income, never assumed to replace her software wage.
She will **verify retirement income** and excludes unoffered class pay and her grown daughter's wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the main wage before a paid cold-chain or college role exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real paid openings and early landlord contact would help protect rent.
